candidates.title: Qualified-help access without case matching
candidates.proposal:
Start with the destination: a visitor seeking legal advice needs usable access instructions for qualified help, but the desk need not first learn their case. Before opening, the volunteers check whether the existing printed information includes a broad legal-help entry point and its published access requirements. This route is usable only where such an entry point is documented; its availability cannot be assumed.

At entry, one volunteer offers: “If you want advice, we can explain how to contact qualified help without hearing your situation. We can also help you use our public information.” Show the same broad access instructions to anyone choosing that route. Do not ask for a legal topic, eligibility history or account of events. Explain only published contact methods, hours and requirements; the qualified service handles its own intake and eligibility decisions. Offer an oral explanation or pointing assistance in the quiet corner. Explain that the corner may be audible before conversation begins.

If the visitor cannot use the published access method, look together for another method explicitly listed in the materials. If none exists, state the unresolved access barrier without promising a referral or collecting private details. Visitors can still receive general printed information. A single arrival-order line covers assistance, with no names or case categories.

The mechanism removes topic matching as a prerequisite for reaching qualified help. Compared with visitor-controlled browsing, it could prevent an uncertain visitor from needing to identify the right legal category first. It requires a documented broad entry point and comprehensible access instructions. It may shift effort to the receiving service or send visitors toward an inaccessible intake process; providing contact details alone does not establish successful access.
candidates.experiment: The welcome volunteer owns a one-opening trial, preceded by a check that the necessary broad entry point exists in print. Alternate this offer with the prior browsing-and-private-assistance route for successive arrivals. Offer an optional, case-free departure check: can the visitor identify a usable next action and explain how to take it? Count unresolved access barriers, assistance time, waiting-order questions and privacy complaints without identifiers or case details. Stop the trial immediately if volunteers need personal facts to choose the destination, or if published instructions do not support the offered route. Reject an improvement claim if navigation is no better or access barriers and assistance burden increase. This tests desk navigation, not whether qualified help is ultimately delivered.

candidates.title: Optional return turns to reduce waiting exposure
candidates.proposal:
Offer visitors a short absence while preserving their place, reducing the time they spend within hearing distance of other conversations. This changes the waiting arrangement rather than requiring visitors to explain why they need privacy.

Before opening, the volunteers identify a conservative return interval within existing hours and agree to allow only one outstanding return turn at a time. At the desk, the welcome volunteer states the service scope and explains the ordinary arrival-order line. When someone would otherwise wait, offer a choice: remain nearby, or return after the stated interval with their place preserved. No name, contact details, reason or registration is required. The volunteer remembers the single outstanding turn and tells later arrivals that one earlier visitor may return ahead of them. The return arrangement must be explained orally, including to visitors who cannot read the scope sheet.

The second volunteer provides public-information assistance in the corner, redirects requests for individualized advice to qualified-help instructions actually present in the materials, and explains any audibility limitation before discussion. Returning visitors receive the next available turn once their earlier place is due; service already underway is never interrupted. A missed return does not freeze the line. Someone arriving later can rejoin, and uncertainty about a return claim is resolved without asking for identifying evidence or case details. Stop issuing return offers sufficiently before closing.

The mechanism reduces simultaneous waiting and opportunities for overhearing. Unlike private-by-default turns, it addresses exposure during the wait itself. It requires reliable volunteer coordination and a queue long enough for leaving to be useful. It offers no guaranteed appointment time and may disadvantage visitors who cannot leave; staying must remain equally available. It cannot compensate for an acoustically inadequate corner.
candidates.experiment: The welcome volunteer owns a trial during one opening period, offering at most one outstanding return turn. Compare with a similar period using ordinary arrival-order waiting and private turns. Tally successful access to assistance, waiting-order questions, missed returns, disputes, extra coordination time and privacy complaints; collect no identities or subjects. Ask departing visitors optionally whether they understood their place and obtained a next step. Stop return offers at the first unresolved place dispute, lost turn attributable to the arrangement, or indication that staying visitors are repeatedly delayed beyond their rightful order. Retain the route only if navigation holds up and reduced waiting exposure outweighs added confusion. Small differences in visitor traffic limit the comparison.
